Belly up (Chrysichthys nigrodigitatus) is a commercially important bagrid catfish widely distributed across West African river systems, where it supports substantial artisanal fisheries. Field surveys conducted in the lower Niger Delta have documented that individuals attain a maximum standard length of 65 cm [Li = 65 cm], placing this species among the larger members of its genus in the region. This ultimate size is achieved through a protracted growth trajectory that spans several years, with the heaviest recorded adults reaching an ultimate wet weight of approximately 2.5 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 2.5 kilograms]. Morphometric analyses based on extensive specimen collections indicate that the relationship between length and mass follows a strongly positive allometric pattern, meaning larger individuals are disproportionately heavier relative to their increase in length. Such size parameters are consistent with those reported for other large-bodied Chrysichthys species inhabiting similar tropical freshwater environments, though local variation in food availability and fishing pressure can influence the maximum sizes observed in any given population.

Reproductive development in Belly up proceeds through a clearly defined size threshold, with field data from the Ouémé River basin indicating that the standard length at puberty is 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 252.6 grams [Wwp = 252.6 grams], derived from length-weight regressions on captured specimens exhibiting mature gonadal tissue. Individuals below this size are typically immature, lacking the developed ovaries or testes characteristic of reproductively active fish. The attainment of sexual maturity appears to be more tightly linked to body size than to chronological age, a pattern commonly observed in tropical siluriforms where growth rates vary considerably with habitat quality and seasonal flooding cycles. Histological examination of gonadal samples from fish spanning the juvenile-to-adult transition has confirmed that ovarian follicular development and testicular spermatogenesis accelerate markedly once individuals cross this 30 cm length threshold.

At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], embryonic development in Chrysichthys nigrodigitatus proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring just 7 days [ab = 7 days] after fertilization. This brief incubation period is typical of many tropical freshwater catfishes that spawn during the warm rainy season, when elevated temperatures accelerate metabolic processes within the developing embryo. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a value consistent with the species' egg diameter of roughly 1.5 millimeters and reflective of a high-fecundity strategy in which numerous small offspring are produced to offset high larval mortality in floodplain environments. At this stage, the prolarvae remain entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves and do not yet exhibit active feeding behavior. The rapid egg development and small neonatal size suggest a reproductive strategy that prioritizes high fecundity and early dispersal over provisioning substantial yolk reserves to each individual offspring.

Reproductive output in Belly up is substantial, reflecting its high fecundity as an iteroparous batch spawner. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], gravid females release approximately 24 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 24 eggs per spawning event] and engage in about 3 spawning events per year [F_R_i = about 3 spawning events per year], yielding a daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.2 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.2 eggs per day]. This high daily fecundity is congruent with the species' spawning strategy, which involves repeated releases of egg batches as opposed to a single massive spawning event. Under the same thermal conditions, the maximum lifespan for Chrysichthys nigrodigitatus is estimated at 6.5 years [am = 6.5 years], based on recapture data from tagged individuals in Lake Volta at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively modest longevity for a fish reaching 65 cm in length is likely shaped by the high natural mortality rates typical of tropical freshwater systems, where predation pressure and seasonal habitat desiccation impose significant constraints on survival.

Field recapture studies indicate a maximum lifespan of 6.5 years [am = 6.5 years], placing Chrysichthys nigrodigitatus among the shorter-lived bagrids relative to its ultimate size, possibly because of the elevated metabolic demands imposed by consistently warm conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The species' life-history strategy is characterized by relatively fast early growth, early attainment of the 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm] standard length at puberty, and high annual reproductive investment, all of which are consistent with a moderate-pace life-history positioned between short-lived opportunistic spawners and longer-lived K-selected species. This suite of traits makes Belly up particularly resilient to moderate fishing pressure, though intensive exploitation of pre-reproductive individuals could erode population stability. Ongoing mark-recapture programs continue to refine estimates of growth parameters and natural mortality rates across its range.
